lines.text: The last topic built a client that handles failure well: a time limit, a shared deadline, a growing wait with randomness, a retry allowance, tripped logic, a repeated key.
None of that actually proves the client is correct. So what does?

lines.text: Here's the smallest test that still earns its keep.
One minimal input, the smallest shape that still exercises the function being checked, not a full dataset of real records.
One call, one check on the shape it hands back. That's the whole test, and it's already enough to catch the one thing it claims to verify.

lines.text: Here's a very different kind of test, built to generate its own inputs rather than take one you hand it.
The same repeated-key rule from the last topic, checked not once but across a hundred separately generated sequences of write attempts, each one varying in length and in which keys repeat.
Every single one of those hundred holds: the number of real effects recorded always equals the number of distinct keys actually used.
Worth guessing at before the reveal settles it.

A handwritten test already sends the same repeated key three separate times and checks that repeating it doesn't double the effect. Does generating a hundred more sequences on top of that actually find anything that handwritten test misses?
It does, and here's precisely why.

A handwritten test only ever exercises the one exact sequence someone sat down and typed. A generated test searches a much larger space of that same rule, including key-reuse patterns nobody thought to write by hand.
Here's a test aimed at an agreement between two separate pieces of code, rather than at one function alone.
The expected request and its minimal expected reply are described once, as a single interaction. From that one description, a real local server is built automatically.
The calling code, with no special awareness that it's being tested, makes a genuine call against that server and gets back exactly the reply the interaction described.
Here's the one layer this sandbox genuinely couldn't run exactly as described, said plainly rather than faked.
The same insert, then read, run directly against this sandbox's own real, already-running database, not an in-memory stand-in that can only ever agree with itself.

The tool built to spin up a disposable copy of that database for every single test needs a container system this sandbox doesn't have. The real database underneath it is still right here, and the test runs against it for real.
One last layer, and it works by comparison rather than by any fresh check.
A fully deterministic report, built from a fixed random starting point, gets written to a file the very first time it runs.
Run it again in the same sitting: nothing new gets worked out, only a comparison against the file already sitting on disk, and that comparison comes back with no difference at all.
Now all five, run together against the exact same client the last topic built.
The minimal-input test, the hundred generated sequences, the agreement check, the real-database check, and the recorded comparison each pass in turn.
Each one was checking a genuinely different claim. None of the other four would have caught what that one specifically catches.
Pulling it all back together now.

A minimal-input test earns its keep on the smallest fixture that still exercises the function. A generated test checks the same rule across a hundred inputs, catching what one handwritten example can't.

An agreement check runs the calling code's real behavior against a server built from a shared description. A real-database check's whole point is a dependency that can genuinely disagree with you — this sandbox ran that part for real, saying plainly that only the disposable-copy tool was unavailable.
And a recorded comparison writes the answer once and checks against it from then on.
One closing scenario, worth reasoning through rather than guessing at.

A team ships a retry client backed only by handwritten minimal-input tests, every one of them passing. Once live, a single repeated key ends up with two real effects recorded against it instead of one — a flaw a hundred generated sequences would have caught on the very first run.
What's actually missing here, and why does an all-green suite of handwritten tests not catch it?
A generated test was missing, and that's the whole answer.

A handwritten minimal-input test only proves the function behaves on the one input it was actually given. It can never prove a rule holds for inputs nobody sat down and wrote — closing exactly that gap is the entire point of a test that generates its own.
